A user asked about media bias detection and used the topic analysis feature. About a minute later they had a list of concepts with citations and links to papers. They called it an 'amazing' tool for literature overviews and for diving into unfamiliar academic domains.

A user tested Elicit on a topic they had researched in depth. It gave mostly incorrect summaries, including claiming a hypothesis was confirmed when it wasn't. It also missed key papers and dug up obscure, irrelevant ones. They later noted it may be geared more to general-public questions.
Elicit quotes sources directly, so you'd expect less hallucination, but it 'still hallucinates just as much'. It then gives a quote that directly contradicts its own statement.

Commenting on Elicit's own guidance to assume about 90% of its information is accurate: one in ten answers being wrong 'just is not good enough for a whole lot of people.' They described that rate as annoying for honest researchers but 'good enough to publish' for dishonest ones.
A user who tested Elicit got 'quite a bit worse results' than with FutureHouse's PaperQA. PaperQA could understand some of the nuance of a scientific query, while Elicit did not.

A user says AI-powered document search engines like Elicit 'just can't stand up to hand picking articles myself.' They also note these tools only cover open-access papers, so paywalled research is missing. For deep dives on individual papers they point to scisummary.com instead.

A user has been disappointed by such research services before because they rely on RAG, which they feel rarely works well for research. They worry it misses very specific ideas, the 'needles in the haystack'.
Search results and the 'Most Relevant Sentence' on the favorites page displayed raw LaTeX syntax (e.g. "$${\text {O}}\bigl (f\bigr )$$") instead of rendered math.

A user ran abstract summarization on Cassandra's CEP-15 whitepaper. It invented facts, such as expanding ACCORD (not an acronym) into a made-up phrase like 'Atomic Consensus by Convex Ordering of Replicated Data'. They asked for the feature to be 'a bit less creative'.
Users complained that Elicit's follow-up email was spam: 'I never signed up for this and was never warned I would sign up or given the option not to.' One user unsubscribed and reported it.
A user said there seemed to be many more features they hadn't tried. They wanted those explained better, with examples, tutorials and more documentation.
The 'Positive reframe' task gave odd output: 'Don't stab me with that knife' became 'There are lots of ways that person can hurt me other than by stabbing me with a knife'.
A user wanted to see more details about what Elicit does before having to sign up.
